samples.summary: `READ_GATED_METHODS` authorizes `AttachDocument` as a read, leaving a repeatable write channel for a viewer-role share link even with enforcement on
samples.evidence: `needWrite = REVISION_READ_METHODS.has(method) ? true : attr.verb === 'rw' && !READ_GATED_METHODS.has(method)` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:332-334) makes `AttachDocument` require only read access, and `hasAccess` then returns `true` for any `yorkie-share` token whose link matches the document, regardless of `link.role` (line 370). Attacker path: a holder of a viewer-role share link calls `POST /auth/yorkie-token/share` to mint a `yorkie-share` Yorkie token, reads `VITE_YORKIE_PUBLIC_KEY` out of the public frontend bundle, builds a bare `yorkie.Client`, applies arbitrary local `doc.update()` changes to a local Document, then attaches — the SDK ships those local changes inside the AttachDocument change pack, which the Yorkie server applies before any `PushPull` is attempted. Detach and re-attach repeats it without bound. The webhook's own comment (lines 99-106) and `docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md` acknowledge this residual, but the branch simultaneously makes enforcement the default and makes several other features (`assertYorkieAuthEnforced` for the public template gallery, `docs/design/sharing.md`'s "Server-side write enforcement") depend on this being the place a viewer's write is refused. It is not, for writes carried by an attach.

samples.summary: An unscoped `yorkie-service` token is a blanket read/write credential for every document in the deployment, and unscoped is the default the minting helpers produce
samples.evidence: `decideService` returns `ALLOW` for any method and any document when the payload carries no `key` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:289-291). The ops scripts mint exactly that: `sideTokenInjector` in `scripts/copy-yorkie-documents.ts:53` and `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv` (`yorkie-service-token.ts:115`, used by `migrate-yorkie-cf-ranges.ts:221` and `migrate-yorkie-worksheet-shape.ts:347`) all call `yorkieServiceTokenInjector(secret)` with no `key`. That token is then handed to the Yorkie SDK and sent to whichever server `YORKIE_RPC_ADDR`/`--target-rpc-addr` names, on every RPC, over a transport the operator chooses (the in-repo default is plaintext `http://localhost:8080`). Because the project public key is not a secret — it ships in every visitor's bundle as `VITE_YORKIE_PUBLIC_KEY` — anyone who captures one of these tokens (server logs, a proxy, a shared/hosted Yorkie, a transcript in CI) can stand up their own SDK client and read and write every document in the deployment for the token's lifetime, with the webhook allowing it by design. Scoping per document (as `YorkieService.withDocument` does) is available but is opt-in; the scripts' comment argues the SDK's refresh timing makes it impractical, which leaves the highest-privilege variant as the one operators actually run.

samples.summary: Service-token scoping fails open: a falsy/empty `key` silently produces the unscoped, all-documents credential instead of an error
samples.evidence: `const payload = key ? { typ, key } : { typ }` (yorkie-service-token.ts:66-68) turns any falsy key — `''`, `undefined` — into the unscoped payload, which `decideService` treats as a blanket allow on every document (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:289). `YorkieService.withDocument` builds the key as `${prefix}${documentId}` with `prefix = options?.docKeyPrefix ?? YORKIE_DOC_KEY_PREFIXES.sheet` (yorkie.service.ts:76-77), so a caller passing `docKeyPrefix: ''` together with an empty `documentId` would escalate a per-request client to a deployment-wide credential with no error anywhere. For a privilege claim the safe direction is the opposite: require the key and make unscoped an explicit, separately named entry point (e.g. `signUnscopedYorkieServiceToken`) so the maximum-privilege token can never be reached by an accidentally-empty string.

samples.summary: A scoped service token is bound to a document but not to a verb or method, so a token minted for a read-only backend attach also authorizes writes and revision restore on that document
samples.evidence: `decideService` compares only `attr.key !== identity.key` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:306-314) and never looks at `attr.verb` or at `REVISION_READ_METHODS`/`RestoreRevision`. `YorkieService.withDocument` mints the same token shape for read paths (`options.syncMode === 'readonly'`, e.g. `ApiV1CellsController.getCells` at cells.controller.ts:88) as for write paths. Since that token is transmitted to the Yorkie server on every RPC, a token captured from a purely read-only backend request grants full read/write — and `RestoreRevision`/`GetRevision` — on that document for its lifetime. Carrying the sync mode in the payload and refusing `rw`/revision methods for a read-minted token would keep the credential's authority equal to the request that created it.

samples.summary: Service-token lifetime is taken from the operator-tunable `YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN` with no upper bound or validation
samples.evidence: `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv` uses `process.env.YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN ?? '10m'` (yorkie-service-token.ts:106) and `YorkieService` does the same from config (yorkie.service.ts:60-62), both cast straight to `ms.StringValue` without validation. That variable is documented as the lifetime of a *user's* short-lived Yorkie token; an operator who lengthens it for UX reasons (e.g. `7d`) silently lengthens the life of the backend service credential too — including the unscoped, all-documents variant the ops scripts mint. The service token's expiry is the main thing bounding a capture, so it should be clamped independently of the user-token setting rather than inheriting it.

verdict.reason: The claimed code exists verbatim. yorkie-auth.controller.ts:108 puts 'AttachDocument' in READ_GATED_METHODS, and lines 332-334 therefore compute needWrite=false for attach regardless of the 'rw' verb Yorkie sends. hasAccess then short-circuits at line 370 (`return needWrite ? link.role === 'editor' : true`), so a viewer-role share link is authorized for an attach whose change pack the Yorkie server applies before any PushPull is evaluated. The vector is reachable: POST /auth/yorkie-token/share exists at auth.controller.ts:82 and mints the share-scoped Yorkie token, the public key ships in the frontend bundle (acknowledged in yorkie-auth-enforcement.ts:5-12), and AttachDocument is the registration the deployment docs instruct operators to add (README.md:211, self-hosting.md:573). DetachDocument is unconditionally allowed (line 66), so detach/re-attach makes the write channel repeatable. I could find no guard anywhere in the repo that inspects or rejects the change pack carried by an attach; the code's own comments (lines 99-106) and yorkie-auth-enforcement.ts:14-21 acknowledge the residual rather than closing it. This is a role check moved out of the enforced path for one RPC, squarely in the authorization lane, and other branch features are documented as depending on this being the enforcement point. Documented-and-intentional does not refute a real viewer-to-writer bypass.

verdict.reason: Every claimed element is present as described. yorkie-auth.controller.ts:289-291 short-circuits to ALLOW for any method and any document key whenever the service-token payload carries no `key`, and it does so as the first statement in decideService, before the per-key comparison at :307 — so nothing downstream bounds it. The minting side matches: signYorkieServiceToken omits `key` by default (yorkie-service-token.ts:66-68), yorkieServiceTokenInjector takes `key` as an optional trailing arg (:82-91), and yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv (:104-116) cannot produce a scoped token at all — it forwards only secret+expiry at :115. The three ops scripts mint exactly that unscoped credential and hand it to a yorkie.Client (copy-yorkie-documents.ts:53, migrate-yorkie-cf-ranges.ts:221, migrate-yorkie-worksheet-shape.ts:347). The scoped variant exists but is opt-in and used only on request paths (yorkie.service.ts:83-87 passes docKey), confirming unscoped is the operator default. Plaintext RPC is a real in-repo default (.github/workflows/ci.yml:590; test helpers default to http://localhost:8080) and the project public key ships client-side, so a captured token is a complete deployment-wide read/write credential for its lifetime. No guard makes the branch unreachable; expiry and JWT_SECRET custody reduce likelihood but not scope. Over-broad credential scope / blanket authorization allow is in the Security lens's authorization lane, so this is not out-of-scope. Confirmed at major severity.
